about: Model Studio (builder T1): one context per model the CED names. Each context unlocks with its topic. The builder report lists what each part checks.
intro:
Every model the exam names, built by hand. Pick a model, see how it works piece by piece, then build it yourself. In Test yourself you build it, apply it to a case and pick out one of its limits.

Models are simplified ideas, not facts: each one here says what it assumes and where it fails.
howItWorks:
Build it. Tap a piece, then the place it belongs (or drag it). Some pieces belong to other models. Check grades every place, and the first mistake is named.

Apply it. A map, a graph or a table to read with the model. Invented places are labeled invented; real places come with the date of what is said about them.

Find a limit. One statement is a real limitation; the others are what the model claims or a misreading of it.

Free: Explore for every model and the demographic transition drills. The other drills are part of Premium.

contexts.name: Demographic transition model
contexts.claim: Birth and death rates fall in sequence as a society changes, so population growth starts slow, speeds up, then slows again. This course shows five stages; some versions of the model show only four.
contexts.origin: A model built mostly from the history of Europe and North America in the 1800s and 1900s.
assumes: Death rates fall first, as food, clean water and medicine improve.
Birth rates fall later, as children survive, more people live in cities and more women go to school and work for pay.

model.title: Demographic transition model: the five stages

slots.name: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Stage 5

pieces.text: High birth rate, high death rate
High birth rate, falling death rate
Falling birth rate, low death rate
Low birth rate, low death rate
Birth rate below the death rate

slips.why: In stage 2 the death rate falls first while births stay high; the birth rate falls in stage 3.
Stage 3 is when the birth rate falls; in stage 2 only the death rate is falling.
In stage 5 births fall below deaths, so the population shrinks; stage 4 has both rates low and close.

decoys.text: Rising birth rate, rising death rate
decoys.why: In the model both rates fall over time; neither rises.

decoys.text: Low birth rate, high death rate
decoys.why: No stage has a low birth rate with a high death rate: the death rate always falls first.

explain.s1: Stage 1: both rates are high, so the population barely grows.
explain.s2: Stage 2: better food, water and medicine cut the death rate, but births stay high, so the population grows fast.
explain.s3: Stage 3: the birth rate falls as more children survive and more people live in cities, so growth slows.
explain.s4: Stage 4: both rates are low and close together, so the population grows slowly or not at all.
explain.s5: Stage 5: births fall below deaths, so without migration the population shrinks. Not every country shows it.

right.t: It was built mostly from European and North American history
right.why: Countries that changed later, such as many in Asia and Africa, moved through the stages faster and in different ways.

right.t: It leaves out migration
right.why: Migration changes a population too, and the model looks only at births and deaths.

right.t: It does not say how long each stage lasts
right.why: The model gives an order, not a timetable, so it cannot say when a country will reach the next stage.

right.t: Not every country with low birth rates shrinks
right.why: Stage 5 is not seen everywhere: some low-fertility countries still grow, through migration or slow change.

claims: The death rate usually falls before the birth rate
Both rates end up low

wrong.t: It shows birth rates rising as a country develops
wrong.why: In the model birth rates fall as a society changes; they do not rise.

wrong.t: It was built from the history of Sub-Saharan Africa
wrong.why: It was built mostly from European and North American history, which is why it fits some other places less well.

contexts.name: Epidemiological transition
contexts.claim: As a society changes, the main causes of death shift from infections and famine to chronic diseases such as heart disease and cancer.
contexts.origin: Abdel Omran first described three stages in 1971; other researchers later added a fourth.
assumes: Better food, clean water and medicine cut deaths from infection first.
People then live long enough for chronic diseases to become the main causes of death.

slots.name: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4

slips.why: Stage 2 is when infections and pandemics recede; chronic diseases take over in stage 3.
Stage 3 is when chronic and human-made diseases become the main killers; in stage 4 they strike at much older ages.

decoys.why: Infant deaths fall through the transition; they do not rise.
The epidemiological transition is about causes of death, not births.

explain.s1: Stage 1: infections, famine and violence cause most deaths, and life is short.
explain.s2: Stage 2: pandemics recede as food, water and medicine improve; deaths fall and life expectancy rises. It matches stage 2 of the demographic transition model.
explain.s3: Stage 3: heart disease, cancer and other chronic and human-made diseases (from smoking or pollution, for example) become the main causes of death.
explain.s4: Stage 4: medicine delays those diseases, so people die of them at much older ages.

right.t: New and returning infections break the sequence
right.why: Pandemics and new or drug-resistant infections can make infectious disease a leading cause of death again.

right.t: Many countries face infections and chronic diseases at once
right.why: Some places have both high infectious disease and rising heart disease, which the stages keep apart.

right.t: It fits the history of richer countries best
right.why: The stages were drawn from countries that went through the change early.

claims: Causes of death shift from infection to chronic disease
Life expectancy rises through the stages

wrong.t: It predicts that infectious disease disappears for good
wrong.why: The model says infections become a smaller share of deaths, not that they vanish.

wrong.t: It describes changes in birth rates
wrong.why: That is the demographic transition model; this one is about causes of death.

contexts.name: Malthusian theory
contexts.claim: Population grows faster than the food supply, so in time food runs short and checks such as famine and disease follow.
contexts.origin: Thomas Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798.
assumes: Population grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8, ...).
Food supply grows arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4, ...).

slots.name: Spot 1: the line that curves upward
Spot 2: the straight line
Spot 3: where the lines cross
Spot 4: the gap after they cross

slips.why: Malthus said population grows geometrically, so its line curves upward; food grows by a fixed amount each period: a straight line.

decoys.why: Critics of Malthus point to the Green Revolution, which raised food output faster than he expected; it is not part of his model.
The demographic transition model is a different model about birth and death rates.

explain.s1: Population grows geometrically: it doubles each period, so its line curves upward.
explain.s2: Food supply grows arithmetically: the same amount each period, so its line is straight.
explain.s3: Where the lines cross, there are more people than food can feed.
explain.s4: After that point, Malthus said, checks such as famine, disease and war bring population back down.

right.t: He did not foresee how much technology would raise food output
right.why: Machines, fertilizer and new crop varieties raised food output far faster than a straight line.

right.t: Birth rates fell as many countries developed
right.why: Population did not keep growing geometrically: fertility fell in many places.

right.t: Much hunger comes from how food is shared, not total supply
right.why: Critics point out that the world grows enough food overall; poverty and conflict keep it from people.

claims: Population grows geometrically
Food supply grows arithmetically

wrong.t: He said food grows faster than population
wrong.why: Malthus said the opposite: population grows faster than food.

wrong.t: He said population can never fall
wrong.why: Malthus said checks such as famine and disease do bring population down.

contexts.name: Ravenstein’s laws of migration
contexts.claim: Patterns in who moves, how far and where: most moves are short, many happen in steps, each flow has a counterflow, and long-distance migrants head for big cities.
contexts.origin: E. G. Ravenstein, papers of 1885 and 1889, built largely on British census data.
assumes: People move mostly for economic reasons.
Distance makes moving harder, so short moves are most common.

model.title: Ravenstein’s laws on a map of an invented region

slots.name: Spot 1: the many short arrows into a nearby town
Spot 2: the chain from village to town to city
Spot 3: the dashed arrow out of the city
Spot 4: the long arrow straight to the city

pieces.text: Most migrants move a short way
Long-distance moves go to big cities

slips.why: Step migration is a chain of shorter moves; the long arrow goes straight to the city in one move.

decoys.why: Ravenstein found that most moves are short.
Ravenstein found that migrants, especially from far away, head for large cities.

explain.s1: Most migrants move only a short distance: the many short arrows.
explain.s2: Migration often happens in steps, from village to town to city.
explain.s3: Each migration flow produces a counterflow: some people move back out.
explain.s4: Migrants who move long distances usually head for large cities.

right.t: It was built on 19th-century British data
right.why: Its laws describe Britain in the 1800s, and patterns differ in other places and times.

right.t: Long-distance and international moves are far larger now
right.why: Cheap travel and global links make long moves more common than Ravenstein saw.

right.t: It says little about forced migration
right.why: Refugees fleeing war or disaster do not follow the economic patterns his laws describe.

claims: Most migrants move a short distance
Each flow produces a counterflow

wrong.t: It says most migrants move to other continents
wrong.why: Ravenstein found the opposite: most moves are short.

wrong.t: It says migrants never return home
wrong.why: One of his laws is that every flow has a counterflow.

contexts.name: Types of diffusion
contexts.claim: A trait spreads from its hearth in two main ways: with people who move (relocation) or while it stays strong at home (expansion), which can be contagious, hierarchical or stimulus.
contexts.origin: A way geographers sort how ideas, goods and practices spread.
assumes: Every trait starts at a hearth, a place where it began.
How it spreads depends on who carries it and through which places.

model.title: Types of diffusion as a tree

slots.name: Spot 1: spreads as the people who carry it move
Spot 2: spreads while it stays strong in its hearth
Spot 3: spreads person to person to nearby places
Spot 4: spreads from big, connected places down
Spot 5: the idea spreads, but the trait changes

slips.why: Relocation diffusion moves with migrants, so it can weaken at home; expansion keeps its hearth strong.
Contagious diffusion spreads to neighbors whatever their size; hierarchical goes from larger, connected places to smaller ones.

decoys.why: Step migration is a kind of migration, not a type of diffusion.
Chain migration is a kind of migration, not a type of diffusion.

explain.s1: Relocation diffusion: the trait moves with migrants, like a language carried to a new country.
explain.s2: Expansion diffusion: the trait spreads outward while it stays strong in its hearth.
explain.s3: Contagious: it spreads to nearby people and places, like a rumor or a disease.
explain.s4: Hierarchical: it spreads from the largest or most connected places to smaller ones.
explain.s5: Stimulus: the idea spreads, but people change the trait to fit their culture.

pool.q: On this invented map of Country A, a new phone app is used first in the Capital Region (1), then in the Eastern Plains and on the South Coast, where the next largest cities are (2), and only later in the rural Northern Hills (3). Which type of diffusion is this?

right.t: Hierarchical
right.why: It moves from the largest, most connected place down to smaller ones, skipping places in between.

wrong.t: Contagious
wrong.why: Contagious diffusion spreads to nearby places in turn; this one jumps from city to city.

wrong.t: Relocation
wrong.why: No one moved: the app spread while staying popular in the capital.

wrong.t: Stimulus
wrong.why: The app itself spread unchanged; stimulus diffusion changes the trait.

map.label: Reference map of invented Country A with numbers showing where a phone app spread first, second and third

pool.q: On this invented map of Country A, a flu starts in the Central Valley (1), spreads to the provinces around it (2), then to a province farther away (3). Which type of diffusion is this?

right.t: Contagious
right.why: It spreads outward to nearby places in turn, like a wave.

wrong.t: Hierarchical
wrong.why: It did not skip from big place to big place; it reached nearby places first.

wrong.t: Relocation
wrong.why: The sick people did not move away; the flu spread to nearby people.

wrong.t: Stimulus
wrong.why: Nothing about the flu changed as it spread.

map.label: Reference map of invented Country A with numbers showing a flu spreading outward from the Central Valley

pool.q: On this invented map of Country A, families from the Northern Hills (A) move to the South Coast (B) and open restaurants there that serve Northern Hills food. Which type of diffusion is this?

right.t: Relocation
right.why: The food spread because the people who cook it moved.

wrong.t: Hierarchical
wrong.why: It did not move down from larger places; it moved with migrants.

wrong.t: Contagious
wrong.why: It did not spread to neighbors in turn; it jumped with the families who moved.

wrong.t: Expansion
wrong.why: In expansion the trait spreads while its carriers stay home; here the carriers moved.

map.label: Reference map of invented Country A with A in the Northern Hills and B on the South Coast

right.t: Real spread usually mixes several types
right.why: A trait can spread through cities first and then to their neighbors, which is hierarchical and contagious at once.

right.t: The internet blurs the types
right.why: Online, a trait can reach many places at once, with little to do with distance or city size.

claims: Relocation diffusion moves with people
Hierarchical diffusion moves from more connected places

wrong.t: Stimulus diffusion copies a trait without changing it
wrong.why: Stimulus diffusion spreads the idea while the trait itself changes.

wrong.t: Expansion diffusion needs people to migrate
wrong.why: That is relocation diffusion; expansion spreads while people stay put.

contexts.name: Boundary types by origin
contexts.claim: Boundaries can be sorted by how and when they were drawn: antecedent, subsequent, consequent, superimposed, relict and geometric.
contexts.origin: A classification geographers use for how political boundaries began.
assumes: A boundary’s type comes from its history: who drew it, when, and around what.

model.title: Six boundaries on an invented continent

slots.name: Spot 1: a straight line along a parallel
Spot 2: drawn before many people settled the area
Spot 3: drawn as the area grew, after people settled
Spot 4: drawn to separate two language groups
Spot 5: drawn by an outside power through a group
Spot 6: the dashed line, no longer a boundary

slips.why: A consequent boundary is a kind of subsequent boundary drawn to follow a cultural divide such as language or religion.
Antecedent boundaries come before most settlement; subsequent ones are drawn after people settle.

decoys.why: Centripetal describes a force that unites a state, not how a boundary began.
An exclusive economic zone is a sea zone under the law of the sea, not a boundary type by origin.

explain.s1: Geometric: a straight line, often along a line of latitude or longitude.
explain.s2: Antecedent: drawn before many people settled there.
explain.s3: Subsequent: drawn after people settled, as the cultural landscape developed.
explain.s4: Consequent: a subsequent boundary drawn to follow a cultural divide such as language or religion.
explain.s5: Superimposed: drawn by an outside power, often ignoring the groups that lived there.
explain.s6: Relict: no longer works as a boundary, but can still be seen in the landscape.

pool.q: The boundary at A follows the 49th parallel between Canada and the United States for much of its length. Which type does that straight line along a parallel make it?

right.t: Geometric
right.why: It is a straight line along a line of latitude.

wrong.t: Relict
wrong.why: It still works as a boundary today.

wrong.t: Consequent
wrong.why: It was not drawn to follow a language or religious divide.

wrong.t: Superimposed
wrong.why: Superimposed is about who drew a line (an outside power, over groups already there), not its shape; the straight line along a parallel is what makes it geometric.

map.label: Reference map of North America with point A on the boundary between Canada and the United States

pool.q: At A, in Berlin, parts of the wall that divided the city from 1961 to 1989 still stand, though the line is no longer a boundary. Which type is it?

right.t: Relict
right.why: It no longer works as a boundary, but it can still be seen in the landscape.

wrong.t: Antecedent
wrong.why: It was drawn in a city where millions of people already lived.

wrong.t: Geometric
wrong.why: It was not a straight line along a parallel or meridian.

wrong.t: Consequent
wrong.why: It did not follow a language or religious divide.

map.label: Reference map of Europe with point A at Berlin, Germany

right.t: One boundary can fit more than one type
right.why: A straight line drawn by an outside power is both geometric and superimposed.

right.t: A boundary’s type can change over time
right.why: When a boundary stops working it becomes relict.

right.t: The types say how a line began, not how it works now
right.why: A boundary’s origin tells us little about whether it is open, closed or disputed today.

claims: A superimposed boundary is drawn by an outside power
A relict boundary no longer works as a boundary

wrong.t: Every boundary fits exactly one type
wrong.why: Many fit two: a straight line drawn by an outside power is geometric and superimposed.

wrong.t: Antecedent boundaries are drawn after settlement
wrong.why: Antecedent boundaries come before most settlement; subsequent ones come after.

contexts.name: Von Thünen model
contexts.claim: Farmers choose what to grow by the cost of moving it to one market, so land use forms rings around the market town.
contexts.origin: Johann Heinrich von Thünen, The Isolated State, 1826, drawn from farming on his estate in northern Germany.
assumes: One market town on a flat, uniform plain with the same soil and climate everywhere.
Farmers carry goods to market themselves, so cost grows with distance.

slots.name: Ring 1 (next to the market)
Ring 2
Ring 3
Ring 4 (outermost)

slips.why: Wood is heavy and was needed every day for fuel and building, so von Thünen put forests in ring 2, closer than grain.
Ranching uses a lot of land and animals can walk to market, so it goes in the outer ring.
Milk and fresh vegetables spoil fast and are costly to move, so they are grown next to the market.

decoys.why: Plantations grow for distant world markets; von Thünen’s rings serve one local market town.
Shifting cultivation is subsistence farming; the model is about farmers selling to one market.

explain.s1: Ring 1: market gardening and dairying. Milk and vegetables spoil fast and are costly to move, so they are grown closest.
explain.s2: Ring 2: forest. Wood is heavy and was needed daily for fuel and building.
explain.s3: Ring 3: grain and field crops, which keep well and are lighter for their value.
explain.s4: Ring 4: livestock ranching, which needs the most land; animals can walk to market.

pool.q: Von Thünen built the model from farming near his estate at A, in northern Germany, in the 1820s. Which change since then most weakens his rings?

right.t: Refrigerated trucks and fast freight move perishable goods far
right.why: Milk and vegetables no longer have to be grown next to the market, so ring 1 can be far away.

wrong.t: Farmers still pay to move crops to market
wrong.why: That is the model’s main idea, so it supports the rings.

wrong.t: Market towns still sell food
wrong.why: A market for food is what the model assumes.

wrong.t: Wood is still used for building
wrong.why: That keeps forests valuable, but it does not break the rings.

map.label: Reference map of Europe with point A in northern Germany, near the Baltic coast

pool.q: Von Thünen also asked what happens if a navigable river runs from the market across the plain. What does that do to the rings?

right.t: They stretch out along the river, where transport is cheaper
right.why: Moving goods by boat costs less, so each land use reaches farther along the river.

wrong.t: They shrink toward the market
wrong.why: Cheaper transport lets each ring reach farther out, not less far.

wrong.t: They stay as perfect circles
wrong.why: A cheaper route changes the cost of distance in one direction, so the circles bend.

wrong.t: All farming moves to the river mouth
wrong.why: There is still one market; the river only lowers the cost of reaching it.

right.t: It assumes a flat, uniform plain with one market
right.why: Real land has hills, rivers, different soils and many markets.

right.t: Refrigerated and fast transport break the rings
right.why: Perishable goods can now travel long distances cheaply.

right.t: Specialty farming regions often break the rings
right.why: Places known for one product, such as a wine region, do not follow the rings.

right.t: Government policy and subsidies change what farmers grow
right.why: Farmers respond to subsidies and rules, not only to transport cost.

claims: Land use depends on transport cost to the market
Perishable goods are grown near the market

wrong.t: It puts ranching next to the market
wrong.why: Ranching uses much land and animals can walk, so it is in the outer ring.

wrong.t: It assumes many market towns
wrong.why: It assumes one market town, which is one of its limits.

contexts.name: Bid-rent theory
contexts.claim: Land users bid more for land with the best access to the center, so the price of land, and how intensely it is used, falls with distance from the CBD.
contexts.origin: An economic theory used for both farmland (Unit 5) and cities (Unit 6).
assumes: One center with the best access.
Each land user pays only as much as access is worth to it.

slots.name: Spot 1: the steepest part, at the CBD
Spot 2: the next part out
Spot 3: the flatter part farther out
Spot 4: the flattest part, farthest out

slips.why: Shops and offices gain the most from being central, so they bid the most at the CBD; housing is farther out.
Retail and offices bid the most for central land, so they are at the steepest part, at the CBD.

decoys.why: Squatter settlements are in the Latin American city model, not one of the bid-rent land uses.
The port zone is part of the Southeast Asian city model.

explain.s1: Retail and offices bid the most for central land, where the most customers and workers can reach them, but their bids fall fast with distance.
explain.s2: Industry bids less than shops, but more than housing.
explain.s3: Housing bids less again, and its bids fall slowly, so it covers a wide band.
explain.s4: Farming bids least, so it is farthest out.

right.t: Many cities have several centers, not one CBD
right.why: Edge cities and suburban centers create more than one peak in land value.

right.t: Zoning laws can block the highest bidder
right.why: A city can keep a use out of a place no matter what it bids.

right.t: Cars and highways change how fast bids fall
right.why: Better transport makes distance matter less, which flattens the curve.

claims: Land users pay more for access to the center
Land use is most intense near the CBD

wrong.t: It says land is cheapest at the CBD
wrong.why: The CBD has the highest bids and the highest land values.

wrong.t: It says housing outbids shops at the CBD
wrong.why: Shops and offices outbid housing at the center.

contexts.name: Rank-size rule and primate city
contexts.claim: In some countries the city ranked n has about 1/n the people of the largest city. Where one city is far larger than the rest, it is a primate city.
contexts.origin: A rule geographers use to compare a country’s cities by size.
assumes: City sizes follow a regular pattern down the ranks.

slots.name: Rank 1
Rank 2

explain.r2: Rank 2 has about half its people.

right.t: It fits some countries, not those with a primate city
right.why: Where one city is far larger, the rule does not hold.

right.t: It depends on where a city’s limits are drawn
right.why: A city proper and a whole metropolitan area give very different sizes.

claims: The city ranked n has about 1/n the people of the largest
A primate city is far larger than the second city

wrong.t: It says every city is the same size
wrong.why: The rule says size falls with rank: the second city has about half the people of the largest.

wrong.t: It says the second city is twice the largest
wrong.why: The second city has about half the people of the largest.

contexts.name: Gravity model
contexts.claim: Interaction between two places (trade, travel, migration) grows with their populations and falls with the distance between them.
contexts.origin: A model borrowed from physics; the version used here is population × population ÷ distance squared.
assumes: Bigger places attract more interaction.
Distance makes interaction harder (distance decay).

slots.name: Most
Least

explain.t0: The pair with the biggest index interacts most.
explain.t2: The pair with the smallest index interacts least.

right.t: Borders, language and culture also shape interaction
right.why: Two big, close cities across a closed border may interact very little.

right.t: New technology changes how much distance matters
right.why: Cheap travel and the internet weaken distance decay.

right.t: It predicts how much interaction, not what kind
right.why: It cannot say whether the flow is trade, tourists or migrants.

claims: Bigger places interact more
Interaction falls with distance

wrong.t: It says interaction grows with distance
wrong.why: Interaction falls as distance grows: distance decay.

wrong.t: It says population does not matter
wrong.why: Population is in the model: bigger places interact more.

contexts.name: Central place theory
contexts.claim: Settlements of different sizes serve market areas shaped like hexagons; bigger places offer higher-order goods that people travel farther for.
contexts.origin: Walter Christaller, 1933, from towns in southern Germany.
assumes: A flat plain with people and buying power spread evenly.
People shop at the nearest place that offers what they need.

slots.name: Spot 1: the center of the largest hexagon
Spot 2: a corner of the largest hexagon’s inner ring
Spot 3: a small dot between those corners
Spot 4: the small shaded hexagon

slips.why: The center of the largest hexagon is the biggest place, offering the highest-order goods.

decoys.why: An edge city belongs to the galactic city model, not central place theory.
A primate city is about one city dwarfing the rest; central place theory is about a hierarchy of market areas.

explain.s1: The city at the center offers high-order goods, such as a specialist hospital, that people travel far for.
explain.s2: Towns offer middle-order goods, such as a shoe store.
explain.s3: Villages offer low-order goods, such as a grocery, bought often and close to home.
explain.s4: Each place serves a market area; hexagons fill the plain with no gaps or overlaps.

right.t: It assumes a flat plain with people spread evenly
right.why: Real land has hills, rivers and uneven population.

right.t: Online shopping changes how far people travel
right.why: People can buy high-order goods without going to a big place.

right.t: Real market areas are not neat hexagons
right.why: Roads, borders and history shape them.

claims: Bigger places offer higher-order goods
Each place serves a hexagon-shaped market area

wrong.t: It says villages offer the most services
wrong.why: Villages are low order; cities offer the most services.

wrong.t: It says market areas overlap and leave gaps
wrong.why: Christaller used hexagons because they fit together with no gaps or overlaps.

contexts.name: Burgess concentric zone model
contexts.claim: A city grows outward from its CBD in rings, with newer and wealthier housing farther out.
contexts.origin: Ernest Burgess, 1925, built on Chicago.
assumes: One CBD at the center.
People move outward as they can afford to, and newcomers settle near the center.

slots.name: Ring 1 (next to the CBD)
Ring 2
Ring 3
Ring 4 (outermost)

slips.why: The commuter zone is the outermost ring; the zone in transition, with factories, is next to the CBD.
Working-class homes sit near the factories of the zone in transition; middle-class homes are farther out.

decoys.why: Edge cities belong to the galactic city model.
The spine belongs to the Latin American city model.

explain.s1: The zone in transition: factories and older, crowded housing next to the CBD, where newcomers often settle.
explain.s2: Working-class homes, close to the factories.
explain.s4: The commuter zone: suburbs whose people travel to the center to work.

pool.q: Burgess drew the model from Chicago (A) in the 1920s. Chicago’s CBD sits on the shore of Lake Michigan. How can the zones fit there?

right.t: Only as half rings on the land side of the CBD
right.why: The lake fills the other side, so the rings can only form inland.

wrong.t: As full circles out into the lake
wrong.why: Homes and factories cannot be built in the lake.

wrong.t: As wedges along the lakeshore
wrong.why: Wedges are Hoyt’s sector model, not Burgess’s rings.

wrong.t: As several separate centers
wrong.why: Several centers is the multiple nuclei model.

map.label: Reference map of North America with point A at Chicago, on Lake Michigan

pool.q: Which change since the 1920s most weakens the model for Chicago (A) and other US cities?

right.t: Cars and highways let homes spread out along roads
right.why: Growth followed highways in some directions, not even rings in every direction.

wrong.t: The CBD still has tall office buildings
wrong.why: A strong CBD at the center fits the model.

wrong.t: Newcomers still find housing near the center
wrong.why: That fits the zone in transition.

wrong.t: Suburbs grew where commuters live
wrong.why: That fits the commuter zone.

map.label: Reference map of North America with point A at Chicago, on Lake Michigan

right.t: It was built on one city, Chicago, in the 1920s
right.why: Other cities, and later times, differ.

right.t: It was drawn before cars spread homes in every direction
right.why: Highways let growth follow roads instead of even rings.

right.t: Real cities grow along transport routes, not even rings
right.why: Rail lines and roads pull growth into wedges.

claims: The CBD sits at the center
Wealthier households live farther out

wrong.t: It puts the commuter zone next to the CBD
wrong.why: The commuter zone is the outermost ring.

wrong.t: It shows land use in wedges along roads
wrong.why: That is Hoyt’s sector model.

contexts.name: Hoyt sector model
contexts.claim: Land use grows outward from the CBD in wedges along transport routes; high-income housing follows the most attractive corridor, and low-income housing sits beside industry.
contexts.origin: Homer Hoyt, 1939, from housing and rent data for 142 US cities.
assumes: One CBD at the center.
A land use that starts along a route keeps growing outward along it.

model.title: Hoyt sectors in a lakeside city

slots.name: Spot 1: the wedge along the rail line
Spot 2: the wedges on both sides of the rail wedge
Spot 3: the wedges next to those
Spot 4: the wedge along the boulevard to the lake

slips.why: High-income housing grows away from industry, along the most attractive corridor; low-income housing sits next to the rail and factories.
The boulevard to the lakeshore is the attractive corridor, so high-income housing grows there.

decoys.why: The commuter zone is a Burgess ring, not a Hoyt sector.
Edge cities belong to the galactic city model.

explain.s1: Industry and warehouses follow the rail line out from the center.
explain.s2: Low-income housing grows beside the industrial wedge.
explain.s3: Middle-income housing lies between low-income and high-income wedges.
explain.s4: High-income housing follows the most attractive corridor, here the boulevard to the lake, away from industry.

pool.q: In invented City B, a boulevard runs north from the CBD along a lakeshore, and a rail line with factories runs south. Where does the sector model expect high-income housing to grow?

right.t: North along the lakeshore boulevard
right.why: High-income housing follows the most attractive corridor, away from industry.

wrong.t: South along the rail line
wrong.why: Industry and low-income housing grow along the rail line.

wrong.t: In an even ring around the CBD
wrong.why: Even rings are the concentric zone model.

wrong.t: In the CBD itself
wrong.why: The CBD is for shops and offices; housing sectors run outward from it.

pool.q: In invented City B, a new rail line with warehouses opens toward the west. What does the sector model expect next to it?

right.t: A wedge of industry with low-income housing beside it
right.why: Industry follows the rail line, and low-income housing grows beside it.

wrong.t: A wedge of high-income housing
wrong.why: High-income housing grows away from industry.

wrong.t: A ring of commuter suburbs
wrong.why: Rings belong to the concentric zone model.

wrong.t: A second CBD
wrong.why: Several centers is the multiple nuclei model.

right.t: It still assumes one CBD at the center
right.why: Many cities grow around several centers.

right.t: It is based on US cities of the 1930s
right.why: Cities elsewhere, and later, grew differently.

claims: Wedges follow transport routes
High-income housing follows the most attractive corridor

wrong.t: It shows zones as even rings
wrong.why: That is the concentric zone model; Hoyt drew wedges.

wrong.t: It puts high-income housing next to industry
wrong.why: High-income housing grows away from industry.

contexts.name: Harris and Ullman multiple nuclei model
contexts.claim: A city grows around several centers (nuclei), not one CBD; some activities cluster together, and others keep apart.
contexts.origin: Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman, 1945.
assumes: Some activities need special sites (a port, a rail yard).
Similar activities gain by clustering; some, like heavy industry and high-income housing, repel each other.

model.title: Multiple nuclei in a drawn city

slots.name: Spot 1: the old center where the main roads meet
Spot 2: beside it, along the rail line
Spot 3: by the river port and the rail line
Spot 4: a second center of shops and offices
Spot 5: far from industry, on the quiet side
Spot 6: out along the rail line, beyond the city

slips.why: Heavy industry and housing on the quiet side repel each other; heavy industry needs the port and the rail line.

decoys.why: The zone in transition is a Burgess ring.

explain.s1: The CBD, where the main roads meet.
explain.s2: Wholesale and light manufacturing, close to the CBD and the rail line.
explain.s3: Heavy industry, at the port and rail yard it needs.
explain.s4: An outlying business district: a second center of shops and offices.
explain.s5: A residential suburb, away from industry.
explain.s6: An industrial suburb, along the rail line beyond the city.

pool.q: In an invented city, a large university and a new airport open far from the CBD. What does the multiple nuclei model expect?

right.t: Each can grow its own cluster of linked activities
right.why: New nuclei attract businesses that gain from being near them.

wrong.t: Everything stays focused on the one CBD
wrong.why: The model says a city has several centers, not one.

wrong.t: The airport becomes a new ring around the CBD
wrong.why: Rings are the concentric zone model.

wrong.t: High-income housing moves next to the airport
wrong.why: Noisy uses tend to repel high-income housing.

pool.q: Why does the model put heavy industry far from high-income housing?

right.t: Some activities repel each other
right.why: Noise and pollution push high-income housing away from heavy industry.

wrong.t: Land near industry is the most expensive
wrong.why: Land near heavy industry is usually cheaper, not more expensive.

wrong.t: The CBD forbids industry
wrong.why: The model is about why land uses cluster or repel, not about rules.

wrong.t: Industry must be in a ring
wrong.why: The model has no rings.

right.t: It does not predict where new centers will form
right.why: It shows that a city has several nuclei, not where the next one goes.

right.t: It is based on US cities of the 1940s
right.why: Cars, suburbs and edge cities changed cities after that.

claims: A city has several centers of activity
Some activities cluster and others repel

wrong.t: It says every city has one center
wrong.why: The model says a city grows around several nuclei.

wrong.t: It shows land use in even rings
wrong.why: That is the concentric zone model.

contexts.name: Galactic city model
contexts.claim: In a car-based metropolitan area, the old central city is one center among many; offices, shops and homes spread along highways and a beltway, with edge cities at the junctions.
contexts.origin: Described for US metropolitan areas in the late 1900s; also called the peripheral model.
assumes: Most people travel by car.
A beltway and highways make places far from the old CBD easy to reach.

slots.name: Spot 1: the old center
Spot 2: where a highway meets the ring road
Spot 3: the areas between highways
Spot 4: the big site with runways

slips.why: Edge cities grow where highways meet the ring road, far from the old center.

decoys.why: The zone in transition is a Burgess ring.
Squatter settlements belong to the Latin American city model.

explain.s1: The old central city is now one center among several.
explain.s2: Edge cities of offices and malls grow at highway junctions on the beltway.
explain.s3: Suburban housing fills the land between the highways.
explain.s4: Airports and business parks are nodes of their own.

pool.q: In an invented US metro with a beltway, where does the galactic city model expect a new edge city of offices and malls?

right.t: Where a highway meets the beltway
right.why: Junctions are easy to reach by car from all over the metro.

wrong.t: In the oldest part of the CBD
wrong.why: The model shows offices and shops spreading out of the old CBD.

wrong.t: Far from any highway
wrong.why: Edge cities need highway access.

wrong.t: In a ring next to the CBD
wrong.why: Rings belong to the concentric zone model.

right.t: It fits US car-based metros better than other places
right.why: Cities built around walking or transit do not spread this way.

right.t: It assumes most people can drive
right.why: People without cars cannot reach jobs spread along highways easily.

claims: Edge cities grow at highway junctions
A beltway ties the metro together

wrong.t: It puts all offices in the old CBD
wrong.why: The model shows offices spread to edge cities.

wrong.t: It is the same as the multiple nuclei model
wrong.why: Both have several centers, but the galactic city model is tied to the beltway and cars.

contexts.name: Latin American city model
contexts.aside: Your class may name its authors, Ernst Griffin and Larry Ford (1980).
contexts.claim: A CBD and a commercial spine with elite housing run out along a main avenue; quality of housing falls toward the edge, where squatter settlements grow.
contexts.origin: A model drawn from many cities in Latin America in the late 1900s.
assumes: Colonial planning centered the city on a plaza and its CBD.
Rapid growth from rural migrants happens at the edge.

slots.name: Spot 1: the center
Spot 2: the wedge along the main avenue
Spot 3: the ring next to the center
Spot 4: the middle ring
Spot 5: the outer ring
Spot 6: the wedge along the river

slips.why: Squatter settlements grow at the edge of the city, where newcomers find land; the ring next to the center is the zone of maturity.
The elite live along the spine near the center, not on the edge.

decoys.why: Edge cities belong to the galactic city model.
The commuter zone is a Burgess ring.

explain.s1: The CBD, often around a colonial plaza.
explain.s2: The spine: a commercial avenue with elite housing along it.
explain.s3: The zone of maturity: older, well-built homes with full services.
explain.s4: The zone of in situ accretion: homes improved bit by bit, with services arriving over time.
explain.s5: Peripheral squatter settlements, where many new migrants build homes.
explain.s6: The disamenity sector: the poorest areas, along rivers, ravines or rail lines.

pool.q: In invented City C, a Latin American city, many new migrants arrive from rural areas. Where does the model expect most of them to build homes first?

right.t: Squatter settlements at the city edge
right.why: Open land at the edge is where newcomers can build.

wrong.t: Along the spine of elite housing
wrong.why: The spine is the most expensive land.

wrong.t: In the zone of maturity
wrong.why: That zone is older, built up and costly.

wrong.t: In the CBD
wrong.why: The CBD holds shops, offices and government buildings.

pool.q: In invented City C, which area does the model expect to have the poorest homes, often along a river or a ravine?

right.t: The disamenity sector
right.why: It is land few others want, so the poorest people live there.

wrong.t: The zone of maturity
wrong.why: That zone has older, well-built homes with services.

wrong.t: The spine
wrong.why: The spine is the elite corridor.

wrong.t: The CBD
wrong.why: The CBD is the commercial center.

right.t: Cities in the region differ a lot from one another
right.why: Each city’s site and history shape it in its own way.

right.t: It may not fit newer suburbs and gated communities
right.why: Wealthy suburbs at the edge break the pattern of poor areas there.

claims: A spine of elite housing runs out from the CBD
Squatter settlements ring the edge

wrong.t: It puts wealthy homes on the city edge
wrong.why: The elite sector runs along the spine near the center; the edge holds squatter settlements.

wrong.t: It has no CBD
wrong.why: The CBD is at the center of the model.

contexts.name: Southeast Asian city model
contexts.aside: Your class may name its author, T. G. McGee (1967).
contexts.claim: Many port cities in Southeast Asia focus on the old colonial port, not one strong CBD, with commercial zones beside it and squatter areas and farmland at the edge.
contexts.origin: A model drawn from port cities in Southeast Asia in the 1960s.
assumes: The colonial port was the reason the city grew.
Trade, not one CBD, organizes the city.

slots.name: Spot 1: at the waterfront
Spot 2: next to the waterfront
Spot 3: scattered at the edge of the city
Spot 4: the band beyond the city

slips.why: The port zone at the waterfront is the city’s focus; squatter areas are scattered at the edge.

decoys.why: The model has no single strong CBD; the old port zone is the focus.
The commuter zone is a Burgess ring.

explain.s1: The old colonial port zone is the focus of the city.
explain.s2: Commercial zones of Western firms and immigrant merchants sit beside the port.
explain.s3: Squatter settlements are scattered at the edge.
explain.s4: Market gardening, small farms selling to the city, lies beyond the edge.

pool.q: In an invented port city in Southeast Asia, where does the model put the focus of the city?

right.t: The old colonial port zone
right.why: The port is why the city grew, so it is the focus.

wrong.t: A single strong CBD in the middle
wrong.why: The model has no single strong CBD.

wrong.t: An edge city at a highway junction
wrong.why: That is the galactic city model.

wrong.t: The band of market gardens
wrong.why: Market gardening is at the edge.

right.t: Cities in the region differ a lot from one another
right.why: Not every city is a port, and each has its own history.

right.t: It reflects the colonial period and may not fit newer cities
right.why: Many cities grew fast after independence and look different.

claims: The port zone is the focus of the city
Commercial zones sit near the port

wrong.t: It shows one strong CBD at the center
wrong.why: The model has no single strong CBD; the old port zone is the focus.

wrong.t: It puts market gardens next to the port
wrong.why: Market gardening is at the edge of the city.

contexts.name: African city model
contexts.aside: Your class may name its author, Harm de Blij.
contexts.claim: Many cities in Sub-Saharan Africa have three central areas side by side (a colonial CBD, a traditional CBD and a market zone), with neighborhoods around them and informal settlements beyond the edge.
contexts.origin: A model drawn from cities in Sub-Saharan Africa in the late 1900s.
assumes: Colonial rule built a separate Western-style center beside an older one.
Rapid growth adds informal settlements at the edge.

slots.name: Spot 1: the center laid out in a grid
Spot 2: the center with winding streets
Spot 3: the area below the two centers
Spot 4: the ring of neighborhoods
Spot 5: the wedge along the rail line
Spot 6: beyond the city edge

slips.why: The grid of high-rise blocks is the colonial CBD; the traditional CBD has narrower, winding streets.

decoys.why: Edge cities belong to the galactic city model.
The zone of maturity is in the Latin American city model.

explain.s1: The colonial CBD: a grid of Western-style blocks.
explain.s2: The traditional CBD: smaller buildings and winding streets.
explain.s3: The market zone: open-air markets and informal trade.
explain.s4: Ethnic and mixed neighborhoods around the centers.
explain.s5: Mining and manufacturing along the rail line.
explain.s6: Informal satellite townships beyond the edge.

pool.q: In an invented city in Sub-Saharan Africa, what does the model expect at the center?

right.t: Three central areas: colonial, traditional and a market zone
right.why: The model has three central areas side by side.

wrong.t: One CBD, like the Burgess model
wrong.why: The model has three central areas, not one.

wrong.t: An old colonial port as the only focus
wrong.why: That is the Southeast Asian city model.

wrong.t: A spine of elite housing
wrong.why: That is the Latin American city model.

right.t: Cities across Africa differ a lot
right.why: A model of a whole region’s cities cannot fit every city.

right.t: It reflects colonial history and may not fit newer cities
right.why: Cities that grew mostly after independence can look different.

claims: Many cities have three central areas
Informal townships grow beyond the edge

wrong.t: It shows one CBD, like a Western city
wrong.why: The model has three: colonial, traditional and a market zone.

wrong.t: It puts mining at the center
wrong.why: Mining and manufacturing run along the rail line, away from the center.

contexts.name: Least cost theory
contexts.aside: Your class may name Alfred Weber (1909).
contexts.claim: A factory locates where its costs of transport, labor and clustering are lowest; a process that loses weight locates near its raw materials, one that gains weight near its market.
contexts.origin: A theory of where factories locate, from the early 1900s.
assumes: Firms only try to keep costs low.
Transport cost depends on weight and distance.

model.title: Least cost: a mine, a market and a port

slots.name: Spot 1: next to the mine
Spot 2: in the market city
Spot 3: at the port, where cargo is unloaded

slips.why: Smelting loses weight, so it is cheaper to process the ore at the mine and ship less.
Bottling adds water and weight, so it is cheaper to bottle near the market.

decoys.why: A software firm ships almost no weight, so transport cost does not tie it to any of these spots.

explain.s1: A weight-losing process (smelting ore) locates near the raw material, so less weight travels.
explain.s2: A weight-gaining process (bottling, which adds water) locates near the market.
explain.s3: A break-of-bulk point, where cargo changes from ship to land, attracts plants that process imports.

right.t: It assumes firms only try to keep costs low
right.why: Owners also choose places for markets, skills or quality of life.

right.t: It leaves out government policy and incentives
right.why: Tax breaks, tariffs and subsidies can outweigh transport cost.

claims: Weight-losing industries locate near raw materials
Weight-gaining industries locate near markets

wrong.t: It puts copper smelters near the market
wrong.why: Smelting loses weight, so it locates near the ore.

wrong.t: It says transport cost does not matter
wrong.why: Transport cost is at the heart of the theory.

contexts.name: Rostow’s stages of economic growth
contexts.claim: Countries develop by passing through five stages, from a traditional farming society to an economy of high mass consumption.
contexts.origin: W. W. Rostow, The Stages of Economic Growth, 1960.
assumes: Every country follows the same path that Western Europe and North America took.
Investment and industry drive growth.

slots.name: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Stage 5

slips.why: Take-off, with rapid growth in a few industries, comes after the preconditions are in place: it is stage 3.

decoys.why: Semiperiphery is a tier of Wallerstein’s world system, not one of Rostow’s stages.
Rostow’s model has no stage where industry declines.

explain.s1: Traditional society: most people farm, with little trade or technology.
explain.s2: Preconditions for take-off: investment, transport and trade begin to grow.
explain.s3: Take-off: a few industries grow fast.
explain.s4: Drive to maturity: industry spreads across the economy.
explain.s5: High mass consumption: most people can buy consumer goods and services.

pool.q: Invented Country D: a few factories making textiles and steel are growing very fast, and investment is rising quickly, but most other parts of the economy are still small. Which stage fits best?

right.t: Take-off
right.why: Rapid growth led by a few industries is take-off.

wrong.t: Traditional society
wrong.why: Factories and fast growth have already started.

wrong.t: High mass consumption
wrong.why: Most of the economy is still small.

wrong.t: Drive to maturity
wrong.why: Industry has not yet spread across the economy.

pool.q: Invented Country E: most people farm by hand for their own needs, trade is small, and new technology is rare. Which stage fits best?

right.t: Traditional society
right.why: Farming for one’s own needs with little trade is stage 1.

wrong.t: Take-off
wrong.why: There is no fast growth in industry yet.

wrong.t: Preconditions for take-off
wrong.why: Investment and trade have not started to grow.

wrong.t: Drive to maturity
wrong.why: There is little industry at all.

pool.q: Invented Country F: most households own cars and appliances, and most workers are in services. Which stage fits best?

right.t: High mass consumption
right.why: Wide ownership of consumer goods is the last stage.

wrong.t: Take-off
wrong.why: Growth is no longer led by a few industries.

wrong.t: Traditional society
wrong.why: Most people do not farm.

wrong.t: Preconditions for take-off
wrong.why: The economy is long past its start.

right.t: It assumes every country follows one Western path
right.why: Countries develop in different ways and orders.

right.t: It ignores how colonialism shaped economies
right.why: Colonial rule built economies around exports to the colonizer.

right.t: It says little about a country’s place in the world economy
right.why: Links to richer countries can hold growth back, as dependency theory argues.

claims: Countries pass through five stages of growth
Take-off brings rapid growth in a few industries

wrong.t: It says countries start at mass consumption
wrong.why: High mass consumption is the last stage.

wrong.t: It sorts countries into core and periphery
wrong.why: That is Wallerstein’s world system theory.

contexts.name: Wallerstein’s world system theory
contexts.claim: One world economy links core, semiperiphery and periphery; the core gains most from the links. Dependency theory and commodity dependence explain why the periphery can stay poor.
contexts.origin: Immanuel Wallerstein, from 1974.
assumes: Countries are tied together in one capitalist world economy.
Tiers are positions in that system, not stages; countries can move between them.

slots.name: Tier 1: Core
Tier 2: Semiperiphery
Tier 3: Periphery

pieces.text: A mix of core and periphery activities
Low wages, raw materials for export

slips.why: The core has high wages and high-tech industry; low-wage raw material exports mark the periphery.

decoys.why: Take-off is Rostow’s stage 3, a different model.
That is von Thünen’s first ring.

explain.s1: The core: high wages, high-tech goods and most of the world’s capital.
explain.s2: The semiperiphery: a mix of core and periphery activities, often industrializing.
explain.s3: The periphery: low wages and raw materials exported to the core.

right.t: Countries are hard to place, since tiers are not measured one way
right.why: Different measures can put a country in different tiers.

right.t: Countries can move between tiers, so any list goes out of date
right.why: A country often classed as periphery can industrialize and move up.

claims: The core, semiperiphery and periphery are linked
Core countries gain the most from the system

wrong.t: It sorts countries by their stage of growth
wrong.why: That is Rostow’s model; Wallerstein looks at links between countries.

wrong.t: It says the periphery is cut off from the core
wrong.why: The model says the tiers are linked in one world economy.
